wsj.summary_analysis: Facebook's second-quarter 2018 report triggered what the article describes as an unprecedented reaction: shares dropped as much as 23% in after-hours trading, a decline that would erase roughly $130 billion in market value if it held -- more, the article notes, than the entire market capitalization of McDonald's. The results themselves were mixed rather than uniformly weak: earnings per share of $1.74 edged past the $1.72 analyst consensus, but revenue of $13.23 billion missed the $13.36 billion analysts had expected, according to Thomson Reuters -- the company's first revenue miss since the first quarter of 2015, as the article specifically notes. Management layered a pointed deceleration warning on top of that miss: executives said the revenue growth rate had already fallen seven percentage points quarter over quarter and would decrease by 'high single-digit percentages' in the second half of 2018, while guiding operating margins down from the quarter's 44% to the 'mid-30s' over the next several years due to higher product and infrastructure spending. User trends in lucrative markets also softened: daily active users in the U.S. and Canada were flat at 185 million, while European daily users slipped to 279 million from 282 million, a decline executives attributed to the new European GDPR privacy law taking effect during the quarter. Zuckerberg himself called the results 'another solid quarter' on the call, but the article notes those comments were 'quickly overshadowed' when other executives detailed the growth deceleration and margin guidance, with SocialFlow CEO Jim Anderson quoted wondering whether the results signaled 'an early warning sign that the market's assumptions about tech companies' growth failed to account for the fact that each of us only has 24 hours in a day.'
wsj.why_moved: The article ties the record plunge directly to the specific combination established above: a rare revenue miss against consensus -- the first since early 2015 -- landing alongside an explicit management warning that revenue growth would keep decelerating by high single digits through the back half of 2018 and that operating margins would compress from 44% toward the mid-30s for years to come. That the softness showed up specifically in Europe, where daily active users actually declined and where executives linked the drop to new GDPR rules, gave the deceleration warning concrete, near-term evidence rather than leaving it as an abstract caution, which the article suggests amplified the market's reaction. Zuckerberg's own characterization of the quarter as 'another solid quarter,' delivered just before the more cautious guidance from his fellow executives took over the narrative, underscores the article's framing that it was the forward-looking guidance and the rare revenue miss -- not the past quarter's underlying growth of 42% -- that investors reacted to so severely.

Facebook Inc. warned that its growth is slowing, sending its stock price plummeting
as investors feared the social-media titan’s fortunes aren’t immune to the multiple
controversies it has faced this year.
After touching record highs earlier on Wednesday, Facebook shares dropped as much
as 23% in after-hours trading, a plunge that would wipe roughly $130 billion from the
company’s value if it holds when the markets open on Thursday. That would be more
than the entire market value of McDonald’s Corp., MCD 1.90% although after-hours
declines don’t always correspond to market prices the next day.

Facebook has shown few business effects from the negative headlines that have
dogged it in recent months. But winding up a quarter during which its privacy
practices stirred fresh controversy, the company late Wednesday reported slower-
than-expected revenue growth for the period—albeit logging in at more than 40%—
and said it expected quarterly revenue growth to decline over the rest of the year.
The Menlo Park, Calif., firm also showed sluggish user trends in some of its most
lucrative markets, including the U.S. and Canada, in the second quarter.
Daily active users in the U.S. and Canada measured at 185 million, flat with the first
quarter and up slightly from a year earlier. Facebook’s daily user base in Europe edged
down to 279 million accounts, from 282 million in the prior quarter. Facebook
executives said that decline stemmed from a tough new European privacy law that
went into effect in the second quarter.
Some worried that the results suggest growth could be threatened not just for
Facebook but also for other tech companies that depend on consumers spending ever-
more time on their digital devices. “I can’t help but wonder if this is an early warning
sign that the market’s assumptions about tech companies’ growth failed to account
for the fact that each of us only has 24 hours in a day,” said Jim Anderson, CEO of
SocialFlow, a platform for publishers to post stories on Facebook and other social-
media sites.
Prior to Wednesday’s report, most analysts expected Facebook to continue its streak
of impressive growth that seemed impervious to controversies about the platform’s
operations.
For the second quarter, Facebook reported earnings per share of $1.74, up from $1.32 a
year earlier. Revenue increased 42% to $13.23 billion. Analysts, on average, expected
earnings of $1.72 a share on revenue of $13.36 billion, according to Thomson Reuters.

advertising products and currency headwinds would clip revenue growth.
They noted that the revenue growth rate fell seven percentage points in the second
quarter compared with the first three months of the year and said the company
expected quarter-to-quarter revenue growth rates to decrease by “high single-digit

The company also said its expenses would rise faster than revenue in 2019 and

The results “showed growth but geographically have pockets of softness,” said Daniel

Facebook’s global reach and impact on the world have been under scrutiny since the

allowing fabricated news articles to flourish on the site.
Those issues intensified in March, when it suspended political analytics firm
